Question: The difference of the squares of two odd numbers is always divisible by \(8.\) If \(a>b,\) and \(2a+1\) and \(2b+1\) are the odd numbers, to prove the given statement we put the difference of the squares in the form:
Solution:
Method 1: Consecutive-integer products

To prove divisibility by \(8\), we can first extract a factor of \(4\) and then show that what remains is even. For integers \(a>b\), expansion and grouping give
\[
\begin{aligned}
(2a+1)^2-(2b+1)^2
&=4a^2+4a-4b^2-4b\\
&=4[a(a+1)-b(b+1)].
\end{aligned}
\]
This is choice \(\text{C}\). Each product of consecutive integers is even, because one of the two integers is even. Thus we may write \(a(a+1)=2r\) and \(b(b+1)=2s\) for integers \(r,s\). The difference of the squares is then
\[
4(2r-2s)=8(r-s),
\]
which is divisible by \(8\).

Choice \(\text{C}\) is therefore a valid proof form. However,
\[
a(a+1)-b(b+1)=(a-b)(a+b+1),
\]
so choice \(\text{D}\) is the same quantity and also supports the proof. The supplied key is \(\text{C}\), but the question does not determine a unique choice.

Method 2: Factor the difference of squares

Factoring the difference of squares gives another direct proof:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(2a+1)^2-(2b+1)^2
&=[(2a+1)-(2b+1)]\\
&\qquad\cdot[(2a+1)+(2b+1)]\\
&=4(a-b)(a+b+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
This is choice \(\text{D}\). The two integer factors inside the product have sum
\[
(a-b)+(a+b+1)=2a+1,
\]
which is odd. They must therefore have opposite parity: if both were even or both were odd, their sum would be even. One factor is consequently even, so their product is \(2k\) for an integer \(k\). The difference of the squares equals \(4\cdot2k=8k\), proving divisibility by \(8\).

Choice \(\text{D}\) is thus a valid proof form. Expanding its product gives \(4(a^2+a-b^2-b)\), also the expansion of choice \(\text{C}\). Thus \(\text{C}\) is valid as well, and the keyed answer \(\text{C}\) is not unique.
